mainTopic: Dreams: their fulfillment, interpretation, and how to respond to them
overview: This amud is mostly about dreams. It opens by finishing the proof from יוסף's dream that even a true dream has a part that does not come true. It then counts 22 years before his dream was fulfilled. רב הונא teaches that a good person is not shown good dreams, and the גמרא works out what this means for someone like דוד. Next comes a procedure for making a troubling dream favorable before three people, using three sets of three verses. אמימר, מר זוטרא and רב אשי then share new teachings: a prayer during ברכת כהנים for a forgotten dream, protection from עין הרע, and when to reveal an illness. The amud ends with ideas about which dreams are true and the power of interpretation (כל החלומות הולכים אחר הפה), and with the teaching that dreams come from a person's own thoughts.

steps.title: יוסף’s mother was no longer alive
steps.stepSummary: The text finishes an earlier explanation: יוסף’s mother was not alive when he had the dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: And at that time, his mother was no longer alive.
steps.whatsHappening: This line completes a point begun on the previous amud. It explains why one detail of יוסף’s dream could not come true literally.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The moon in the dream represented יוסף’s mother, but she was no longer alive. A dream can therefore come true overall without every detail happening literally.

phrases.english: And at that time, his mother was no longer alive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues an explanation begun on the previous amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why a detail of the dream could not be fulfilled literally.
steps.terutzMaskana: יוסף’s mother was no longer alive at the time of the dream.

steps.title: Keep expecting a good dream for twenty-two years
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי says that a person should keep hoping for a good dream to come true for as long as twenty-two years.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי לוי said: A person should always anticipate the fulfillment of a good dream for up to twenty-two years.
steps.whatsHappening: The text moves from a detail of יוסף’s dream to a new teaching about how long a good dream may take to come true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A long delay does not, by itself, mean the dream will not come true. The next step looks for the source of the twenty-two-year period.

phrases.english: Rabbi Levi said:
A person should always anticipate a good dream
for up to twenty-two years.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי לֵוִי: לְעוֹלָם יְצַפֶּה אָדָם לַחֲלוֹם טוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the earlier detail of יוסף’s dream to a teaching drawn from its timing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Keep anticipating a good dream for up to twenty-two years.

steps.title: The two verses that begin the calculation
steps.stepSummary: The text asks for רבי לוי’s source and points to verses that give יוסף’s age at two stages of his story.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where do we learn this? From יוסף: one verse says he was seventeen, and another says he was thirty when he stood before פרעה.
steps.whatsHappening: The question asks where the twenty-two-year figure comes from. The answer begins with two verses about יוסף’s age, setting up the calculation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first verse places יוסף at seventeen near the start of the story. The second places him at thirty before פרעה; the text has not yet added the later years.

phrases.english: Where do we learn this? From Joseph, as it is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״אֵלֶּה תֹּלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב יוֹסֵף בֶּן שְׁבַע עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה וְגוֹ׳״,
phrases.english: “These are the generations of Jacob; Joseph was seventeen years old, etc.”
And it is written: “Joseph was thirty years old
when he stood before Pharaoh, etc.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins to support רבי לוי’s twenty-two-year figure with verses.
steps.raayaObject: The time between יוסף’s dream and its fulfillment.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Verses describing יוסף at age seventeen and at age thirty.

steps.title: The years add up to twenty-two
steps.stepSummary: Thirteen years to יוסף’s rise, seven years of plenty, and two years of famine make twenty-two years.
steps.simpleTranslation: How many years are there from seventeen to thirty? Thirteen. Add seven years of plenty and two of famine: that makes twenty-two.
steps.whatsHappening: The text now does the arithmetic promised by the verses. It reaches the twenty-two years stated by רבי לוי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From seventeen to thirty is thirteen years. Adding seven years of plenty and two years of famine gives twenty-two, the time before יוסף’s brothers bowed to him.

phrases.aramaic: מִן שַׁבְסְרֵי עַד תְּלָתִין כַּמָּה הָוֵי? —
phrases.english: From seventeen to thirty, how many years is that?
Thirteen,
plus seven of plenty and two of famine—
that makes twenty-two.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִן שַׁבְסְרֵי עַד תְּלָתִין כַּמָּה הָוֵי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the calculation begun with the two verses.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: יוסף’s story supplies רבי לוי’s twenty-two-year period.

steps.title: Good and bad people are shown different dreams
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא says that a good person is not shown a good dream, while a bad person is not shown a bad dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: A good person is not shown a good dream, and a bad person is not shown a bad dream.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching turns from when a dream comes true to what kind of dream a person is shown.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The statement deliberately contrasts the person’s character with the dream’s content. The next line gives named examples that support it.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:

phrases.aramaic: לְאָדָם טוֹב אֵין מַרְאִין לוֹ חֲלוֹם טוֹב,
phrases.english: A good person is not shown a good dream,

phrases.aramaic: וּלְאָדָם רַע אֵין מַרְאִין לוֹ חֲלוֹם רַע.
phrases.english: and a bad person is not shown a bad dream.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a separate teaching about dreams.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A good person is not shown a good dream, and a bad person is not shown a bad dream.

steps.title: דוד and אחיתופל illustrate the teaching
steps.stepSummary: A supporting teaching says דוד never saw a good dream, while אחיתופל never saw a bad dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was also taught: Throughout all his years, דוד did not see a good dream, and throughout all his years, אחיתופל did not see a bad dream.
steps.whatsHappening: A previously taught statement supports רב הונא with two examples. דוד matches the good-person side, and אחיתופל matches the bad-person side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The examples repeat the same contrast rather than adding a new rule. They show how the statement about good and bad dreams applies to named people.

phrases.english: This was also taught:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל שְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל דָּוִד לֹא רָאָה חֲלוֹם טוֹב,
phrases.english: Throughout all of David’s years, he did not see a good dream,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל שְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל אֲחִיתוֹפֶל לֹא רָאָה חֲלוֹם רַע.
phrases.english: and throughout all of Ahitophel’s years, he did not see a bad dream.

steps.whatToRemember: The teaching pairs דוד with the absence of good dreams and אחיתופל with the absence of bad dreams.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב הונא’s statement with two named examples.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא’s contrast between dreams shown to good and bad people.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A teaching about דוד and אחיתופל.

steps.title: A verse challenges the earlier teaching about dreams
steps.stepSummary: A verse promises protection from evil, and an explanation of the verse includes protection from frightening dreams.
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn’t it written, “No evil will befall you”? רב חסדא, citing רב ירמיה בר אבא, explains that this means neither bad dreams nor bad thoughts will frighten you. The verse also says that no plague will approach your tent; this is explained as not finding your wife in a state of uncertain נדה when you return from a journey.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a verse that seems hard to fit with the earlier account of who sees which dreams. It quotes an explanation that specifically promises protection from frightening dreams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier teaching left the good person without good dreams. This verse appears to protect such a person from frightening bad dreams too, so the גמרא needs a more precise account.

keyTerms.meaning: uncertain status as a menstruating woman

phrases.english: But isn’t it written: “No evil will befall you”?

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב חִסְדָּא אָמַר רַב יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: And Rav Ḥisda said in the name of Rav Yirmeya bar Abba:
That bad dreams will not frighten you,
nor will bad thoughts.
“And no plague will come near your tent”—
that you will not find your wife of uncertain menstrual status
when you return from a journey.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the picture of dreams presented in the preceding teaching and its support.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier teaching about which dreams a good person sees.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The cited explanation of the verse promises protection from frightening bad dreams.

steps.title: Others may see the dream instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא distinguishes between the person seeing a dream and others seeing a dream about that person.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, he himself does not see it; others see it concerning him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a distinction: the person does not personally see the dream, but other people do. This is its first attempt to resolve the difficulty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proposed answer narrows the earlier language about seeing dreams. It moves the dream experience from the person himself to other people.

phrases.english: Rather, he himself does not see it,
but others see it concerning him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a distinction in response to the verse.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the person who is the subject of a dream from the person who sees it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The person personally sees the dreams under discussion.
steps.terutzMaskana: Other people can see dreams concerning him even when he does not see them himself.

steps.title: Is having no dreams a good sign?
steps.stepSummary: A teaching about seven dreamless days challenges the proposed answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he does not see a dream, is that a virtue? רבי זעירא said that anyone who sleeps seven days without a dream is called “bad.” He supports this with a verse and reads its word for “satisfied” as “seven.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that not seeing a dream is an advantage. It cites רבי זעירא’s teaching about seven days without a dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous answer treated not seeing a dream as protection. This teaching makes an extended absence of dreams sound negative, so that answer needs to be refined.

keyTerms.meaning: do not read it as; an introduction to a different reading

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי לָא חֲזָא אִיהוּ, מְעַלְּיוּתָא הוּא?
phrases.english: And if he himself does not see a dream, is that an advantage?
But didn’t Rabbi Zeira say:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַלָּן שִׁבְעָה יָמִים בְּלֹא חֲלוֹם —
phrases.english: Anyone who sleeps seven days without a dream—
is called “bad.”
As it says: “And one who is satisfied will sleep; he will not be visited by evil.”
Do not read “satisfied,” but “seven.”

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי לָא חֲזָא אִיהוּ, מְעַלְּיוּתָא הוּא?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the implication that seeing no dream is itself beneficial.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the person himself does not see the dream.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי זעירא calls seven days without a dream a bad sign, not a virtue.

steps.title: He dreams but does not know what he saw
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא revises the earlier description: the person does have a dream but cannot recall or identify its contents.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what it means: He sees a dream but does not know what he saw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא replaces the idea that the person sees no dream. He dreams, but he does not know what he saw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This preserves the distinction from someone who goes without a dream. The missing part is his knowledge of the dream’s content, not the dream itself.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what it means:
He saw a dream but did not know what he saw.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Refines the earlier answer so it does not require the person to be dreamless.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the description of not seeing a dream.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He does not experience a dream.
steps.terutzMaskana: He experiences a dream but does not know what he saw.
steps.whatToRemember: The distinction is between having no dream and having a dream whose contents you do not know.

steps.title: An initial instruction for someone troubled by a dream
steps.stepSummary: A new teaching says that a person upset by a dream should bring it before three people for interpretation.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא בר אמי said in the name of רבי פדת, who said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Someone who sees a dream and feels distressed should go and have it interpreted before three people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new discussion: what should a person do when a dream leaves them distressed? The first wording says to have the dream interpreted before three people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is an instruction about responding to a troubling dream, not a claim about which people have dreams. The next step will examine the word “interpreted.”

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי פְּדָת אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rav Huna bar Ami said in the name of Rabbi Pedat, who said in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan:
One who sees a dream and feels distressed
should go and have it interpreted before three.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא בַּר אַמֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי פְּדָת אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from understanding dream experiences to responding to a distressing dream.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: As initially worded, a distressed dreamer should have the dream interpreted before three people.

steps.title: Why seek an interpretation?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the instruction to interpret the dream by citing a comparison between an uninterpreted dream and an unread letter.
steps.simpleTranslation: “Have it interpreted”?! But didn’t רב חסדא say that a dream not interpreted is like a letter not read?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the word “interpreted.” It brings רב חסדא’s teaching that an uninterpreted dream is like an unread letter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An unread letter has not yet delivered its message. For someone already worried about a dream, seeking an interpretation seems an odd first instruction.

phrases.english: “Have it interpreted”?!
But didn’t Rav Ḥisda say
that a dream not interpreted
is like a letter not read?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the instruction to seek an interpretation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word “וְיִפְתְּרֶנּוּ” in the preceding instruction.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב חסדא compares an uninterpreted dream to an unread letter, making active interpretation a questionable response to a distressing dream.

steps.title: The instruction is to make the dream favorable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא corrects the instruction: the dreamer should have the dream made favorable before three people.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: He should make it favorable before three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא replaces “have it interpreted” with “make it favorable.” It keeps the instruction to do this before three people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three people are not being asked to find a hidden meaning in the dream. The following lines spell out what they and the dreamer should say.

phrases.english: Rather, say:
He should make it favorable before three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Corrects the word challenged in the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the stated action with a different action.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The dreamer should seek an interpretation.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dreamer should make the dream favorable before three people.

steps.title: What the dreamer and the three people say
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the words for making a dream favorable and then directs the three people to recite three groups of verses.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should bring three people and tell them, “I saw a good dream.” They respond, “It is good, and may it be good. May the Merciful One make it good. May they decree for you from heaven seven times that it be good, and may it be good.” They then say three verses of transformation, three of redemption, and three of peace.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the procedure promised in the corrected instruction. The dreamer speaks first, the three respond, and they then say three sets of verses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The response repeatedly asks that the dream turn out well. The text names the three kinds of verses here; it begins listing the verses in the next step.

phrases.english: Let him bring three and say to them:
“I saw a good dream.”
And those people should say to him:
“It is good, and may it be good;
may the Merciful One make it good.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁבַע זִימְנִין לִגְזְרוּ עֲלָךְ מִן שְׁמַיָּא
phrases.english: May they decree for you from heaven seven times
that it be good, and may it be good.”
And they should say three transformations,
three redemptions, and three expressions of peace.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how to carry out the instruction to make the dream favorable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The dreamer and three others say the specified words, followed by three groups of verses.

steps.title: The three verses about transformation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lists the three verses in the first group: each describes a turn from something painful to something good.
steps.simpleTranslation: The three transformations are: “You turned my mourning into dancing for me; You loosened my sackcloth and clothed me with joy”; “Then a young woman will rejoice in dancing, and young men and old men together; I will turn their mourning into joy, etc.”; and “ה׳ your God did not wish to listen to בלעם, and He turned, etc.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fills in the first group of verses named in the procedure: the three transformations. The redemption verses follow in Step 16 and the peace verses in Step 17.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each quoted verse contains a change toward a better outcome. That is why these verses belong to the transformation group.

phrases.english: The three transformations are—
“You turned my mourning into dancing for me;
You loosened my sackcloth and girded me with joy”;
“Then a young woman will rejoice in dancing,
and young men and old men together;
and I will turn their mourning into joy, etc.”;
“And the Lord your God did not wish
to listen to Balaam, and He turned, etc.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the verses for the first of the three named groups.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first group consists of three verses about transformation toward a good outcome.

steps.title: The second group: three verses of redemption
steps.stepSummary: The second group of verses for making a dream favorable is three verses that mention redemption or rescue.
steps.simpleTranslation: Three redemptions, as it is written: 'He redeemed my soul in peace from the battle against me, etc.'; 'The redeemed of ה׳ shall return, etc.'; 'And the people said to שאול: Shall יונתן die, who brought about this salvation, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the list of verses the three people say. This is the second group: three verses about being redeemed or rescued.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each verse describes someone saved from danger: the speaker of תהילים saved from battle, the Jewish people returning to ציון, and יונתן rescued from a death sentence. Saying these verses asks that any danger in the dream be undone in the same way.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a verse)

phrases.english: Three redemptions, as it is written:
'He redeemed my soul in peace
from the battle against me, etc.' (תהילים 55:19);
'The redeemed of Hashem shall return, etc.' (ישעיהו 35:10);
'And the people said to Shaul:
Shall Yonatan die,
who brought about the salvation, etc.' (שמואל א 14:45).
phrases.notes: The verse ends: 'So the people rescued יונתן.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list started in Step 15 by giving the second of the three verse groups.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The second group said for making a dream favorable is three verses of redemption.

steps.title: The third group: three verses of peace
steps.stepSummary: The third and last group is three verses that mention שלום.
steps.simpleTranslation: Three mentions of peace, as it is written: 'I create the speech of the lips: Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, says ה׳, and I will heal him'; 'And a spirit came upon עמשי, etc.'; 'And you shall say: Thus to life, and peace to you, and peace to your house, etc.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the list with the third group of verses, all about שלום. This completes the procedure for making a dream favorable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each verse blesses someone with peace. The first even promises healing, which fits a dream that needs to be 'healed.' Ending with peace asks that the dream bring only calm and good.
steps.confusionAlert: In the עמשי verse, the words 'peace, peace to you' come in the part covered by וגו׳. The גמרא quotes only the opening, but the peace is in the rest of the verse.
steps.whatToRemember: Making a dream favorable has three parts: three people, words of blessing, and three groups of three verses: turning (bad to good), redemption, and peace.

phrases.english: Three mentions of peace, as it is written:
'I create the speech of the lips:
Peace, peace, to the far and to the near,
says Hashem, and I will heal him' (ישעיהו 57:19);
'And a spirit came upon Amasai, etc.' (דברי הימים א 12:19);
phrases.notes: The verse continues: 'peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers.'

phrases.english: 'And you shall say: Thus, to life,
and peace to you, and peace to your house, etc.' (שמואל א 25:6).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the third and final verse group, closing the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The third group said for making a dream favorable is three verses of peace.

steps.title: Three sages agree to each share something new
steps.stepSummary: A story begins: אמימר, מר זוטרא, and רב אשי sat together and agreed that each would say something the others had not heard.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר, מר זוטרא, and רב אשי were sitting together. They said: Let each one of us say something that his friend has not heard.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא introduces a gathering of three sages and prepares us for the teachings each one will share.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No ruling is given here. It sets up a series of new teachings, and the first one continues the topic of dreams.

phrases.english: Ameimar and Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi
were sitting together.
They said: Each and every one of us
should say a teaching
that his friend has not heard.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַמֵּימָר וּמָר זוּטְרָא וְרַב אָשֵׁי הֲווֹ יָתְבִי בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story that will bring more teachings, beginning with another dream practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative setup: three sages agree to share new teachings.

steps.title: A prayer during ברכת כהנים for a forgotten dream
steps.stepSummary: The first sage teaches that someone who dreamed but does not know what he saw should stand before the כהנים during ברכת כהנים and pray. The prayer begins by asking that good dreams be strengthened like יוסף's.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of them began and said: Someone who saw a dream and does not know what he saw should stand before the כהנים when they spread their hands and say: 'Master of the world, I am Yours and my dreams are Yours. I dreamed a dream and I do not know what it is. Whether I dreamed about myself, my friends dreamed about me, or I dreamed about others: if they are good, strengthen them and make them firm like the dreams of יוסף.'
steps.whatsHappening: The first sage shares his new teaching: what to do about a dream you cannot remember. He gives the timing (during ברכת כהנים) and the first part of the prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the dreamer knew his dream and brought it to three people. Here he does not even know what he dreamed, so he hands the whole matter to ה׳. The prayer covers every kind of dream and first asks that the good ones come true, like יוסף's dreams did.

keyTerms.meaning: When they spread their hands (during ברכת כהנים)
Strengthen them and make them firm

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source of the רבונו של עולם prayer that many say during ברכת כהנים to this day.

phrases.english: One of them began and said:
One who saw a dream
and does not know what he saw
should stand before the priests
at the time when they spread their hands
and say as follows:
'Master of the world,
I am Yours and my dreams are Yours.

phrases.aramaic: חֲלוֹם חָלַמְתִּי וְאֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ מַה הוּא.
phrases.english: I dreamed a dream and I do not know what it is.
Whether I dreamed about myself,
or my friends dreamed about me,
or I dreamed about others,
if they are good, strengthen them and make them firm
like the dreams of Yosef.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first sage delivers the new teaching promised in Step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person who does not know what he dreamed should pray during ברכת כהנים that good dreams be strengthened like יוסף's.

steps.title: The prayer continues: heal bad dreams and turn them to good
steps.stepSummary: The prayer continues: if the dreams need healing, heal them as ה׳ healed in famous stories, and turn them to good as He turned בלעם's curse into a blessing.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And if they need healing, heal them like the waters of מרה through משה רבינו, like מרים from her צרעת, like חזקיהו from his illness, and like the waters of יריחו through אלישע. And just as You turned the curse of בלעם the wicked into a blessing, so turn all my dreams about me to good.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the same prayer. It deals with dreams that might be bad.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each example is something harmful that ה׳ healed: bitter water made sweet, צרעת cured, a deadly illness cured, bad water fixed. The last example, בלעם, goes further: the curse did not just stop, it became a blessing. That is the request for the dreams.

phrases.english: And if they need healing,

phrases.aramaic: רְפָאֵם כְּמֵי מָרָה עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ,
phrases.english: heal them like the waters of Marah through Moshe our teacher,
and like Miriam from her tzaraas,
and like Chizkiyahu from his illness,
and like the waters of Yericho through Elisha.

phrases.aramaic: וּכְשֵׁם שֶׁהָפַכְתָּ קִלְלַת בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע לִבְרָכָה,
phrases.english: And just as You turned the curse of Bilam the wicked into a blessing,

phrases.aramaic: כֵּן הֲפוֹךְ כׇּל חֲלוֹמוֹתַי עָלַי לְטוֹבָה״.
phrases.english: so turn all my dreams about me to good.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same prayer, moving from good dreams to dreams that need healing.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The prayer asks that bad dreams be healed and turned to good, like בלעם's curse.

steps.title: Timing the ending with the כהנים, and a short backup prayer
steps.stepSummary: The dreamer should finish his prayer together with the כהנים so the congregation's אמן covers it too. If he cannot say the full prayer, he says a short prayer for שלום.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should finish together with the כהנים, so that the congregation answers 'אמן.' And if not, he should say: 'Mighty One on high, Who dwells in power, You are peace and Your name is peace. May it be Your will that You place peace upon us.'
steps.whatsHappening: The first sage adds two practical details. Time the prayer to end with the כהנים' blessing, and if you cannot manage the long version, say a short one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ending together with the כהנים means the congregation's אמן answers both their blessing and his private request. The short backup prayer is built around שלום, fitting the theme of ברכת כהנים, which ends with peace.
steps.whatToRemember: For a dream you cannot remember: say רבונו של עולם during ברכת כהנים, end with the כהנים so the congregation's אמן covers it, or say the short אדיר במרום prayer.

phrases.english: And he should finish together with the priests
so that the congregation answers 'Amen.'
And if not, he should say as follows:
'Mighty One on high, Who dwells in power,
You are peace and Your name is peace.
May it be Your will
that You place peace upon us.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְסַיֵּים בַּהֲדֵי כָּהֲנֵי דְּעָנֵי צִבּוּרָא אָמֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the first sage's teaching with timing guidance and a shorter alternative.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Finish the prayer with the כהנים so the congregation's אמן covers it; otherwise say the short אדיר במרום prayer.

steps.title: Protection from עין הרע when entering a city
steps.stepSummary: The second sage teaches that someone entering a city who fears עין הרע should hold his thumbs and declare that he comes from the descendants of יוסף, whom עין הרע cannot harm. A verse read in a new way is the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The other began and said: Someone who enters a city and fears עין הרע should hold the thumb of his right hand in his left hand and the thumb of his left hand in his right hand and say: 'I, so-and-so son of so-and-so, come from the descendants of יוסף, over whom עין הרע has no power,' as it says: 'יוסף is a fruitful son, a fruitful son by a fountain (עלי עין).' Do not read עלי עין but עולי עין: those who rise above the eye.
steps.whatsHappening: The second sage shares his new teaching, on a new topic. He gives an action, words to say, and a verse as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The protection depends on the claim that יוסף's descendants are immune to עין הרע. The source is a אל תקרי reading: 'by the fountain' (עלי עין) is reread as 'rising above the eye' (עולי עין), meaning above the reach of the evil eye.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not read it as... (a rereading of a verse to teach a lesson)
Those who rise above the eye

steps.confusionAlert: אל תקרי does not mean the written text of the תורה is changed. It is a way of finding an extra lesson by reading the same letters differently.

phrases.english: The other began and said:
One who enters a city
and fears the evil eye
should hold the thumb of his right hand
in his left hand
and the thumb of his left hand
in his right hand,
and say as follows:
I, so-and-so son of so-and-so,
come from the descendants of Yosef,
over whom the evil eye has no power,
as it is stated: 'Yosef is a fruitful son,
a fruitful son by a fountain, etc.' (בראשית 49:22).
Do not read it as 'alei ayin' (by a fountain),
but rather 'olei ayin' (rising above the eye).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The second sage begins his new teaching, switching from dreams to עין הרע.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who fears עין הרע on entering a city holds his thumbs and declares he is from יוסף's descendants, who rise above the evil eye.

steps.title: A second source: יוסף's descendants are like fish
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא brings a different verse to show that יוסף's descendants are protected from עין הרע: they are blessed to multiply like fish, which are hidden under water.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: From here: 'And may they multiply like fish in the midst of the land.' Just as fish in the sea are covered by water and עין הרע has no power over them, so too יוסף's descendants: עין הרע has no power over them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second, different source for the same idea, that עין הרע cannot harm יוסף's descendants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The conclusion stays the same. Only the proof-verse changes. The verse in יעקב's blessing to יוסף's sons uses a word related to דגים (fish). Fish live hidden under water where no eye sees them, so the evil eye cannot reach them, and the same is true of יוסף's offspring.

keyTerms.meaning: And may they multiply (like fish, דגים)

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא אָמַר, מֵהָכָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina said: From here:
'And may they multiply like fish in the midst of the land' (בראשית 48:16).
Just as fish in the sea,
water covers them
and the evil eye has no power over them,
so too the descendants of Yosef:
the evil eye has no power over them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא אָמַר, מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different verse as the source for the same claim made in Step 22.
steps.raayaObject: That עין הרע has no power over יוסף's descendants.
steps.raayaSupportSource: בראשית 48:16, 'וידגו לרב': like fish hidden under water, they are hidden from the evil eye.

steps.title: If he fears his own evil eye
steps.stepSummary: If a person worries that his own eye might harm others, he should look at the side of his left nostril.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he fears his own evil eye, he should look at the side of his left nostril.
steps.whatsHappening: The second sage adds the flip side: what to do if you worry that you might be the one giving עין הרע to others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps protected a person from other people's eyes. This step turns to the danger of his own eye harming others. The advice is to look down at his own left nostril, which keeps his gaze from resting on what belongs to others.
steps.whatToRemember: Against other people's עין הרע: hold your thumbs and declare you are from יוסף. Against your own: look at the side of your left nostril.

phrases.english: And if he fears his own evil eye,
he should look at the side of his left nostril.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the reverse case to the second sage's teaching: guarding others from one's own eye.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who fears his own evil eye should look at the side of his left nostril.

steps.title: Do not reveal an illness on the first day
steps.stepSummary: Another sage teaches that a sick person should keep his illness private on the first day so that his מזל is not weakened. After that, he may reveal it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another one began and said: A person who becomes sick should not tell anyone on the first day, so that his luck is not damaged. From then on, he should tell people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the next sage's practical advice in the series. This one is about what a sick person should do on the first day of his illness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Publicizing a fresh illness may 'set' it as his fate, so a quiet first day protects his מזל. After the first day the illness is already established, so he gains more by letting people know and pray for him.

keyTerms.meaning: the other one (another of the sages in the group)

phrases.english: Another began and said:
One who is sick,
on the first day should not reveal it,
so that his luck should not be weakened;
phrases.notes: מזל here means a person's fortune or fate.

phrases.english: from then on, he should reveal it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of practical sayings, with a new sage and a new topic: illness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hide an illness on the first day. Reveal it afterward.

steps.title: רבא's practice when he got sick
steps.stepSummary: רבא followed this exact practice. He kept quiet on the first day, and then he had his attendant announce that he was sick, so friends would pray and enemies would rejoice.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like רבא's practice. When he got sick, he did not reveal it on the first day. From then on, he told his attendant: Go out and announce, 'רבא is sick.' Whoever loves me should pray for mercy for me, and whoever hates me should rejoice over me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the previous saying with a real-life example from רבא. It also adds why he wanted the news spread after the first day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's practice matches both halves of the rule: silence on day one, then publicity. The surprising part is that he wanted even his enemies to hear about it. The next step explains why.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not asking people to sin by hating him. He simply knows that some people dislike him, and he wants even their reaction to end up helping his recovery.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרָבָא, כִּי הֲוָה חֲלִישׁ,
phrases.english: Like that of Rava: when he was sick,
on the first day he would not reveal it;
from then on he would say to his attendant:
Go out and announce: 'Rava is sick.'

phrases.aramaic: מַאן דְּרָחֵים לִי — לִבְעֵי עֲלַי רַחֲמֵי,
phrases.english: Whoever loves me should pray for mercy on me,
and whoever hates me should rejoice over me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rule in Step 25 with רבא's personal practice.
steps.raayaObject: The rule to hide an illness on the first day and reveal it afterward
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבא's own conduct when he was sick

steps.title: Why an enemy's joy can help the sick person
steps.stepSummary: A verse in משלי shows that when an enemy rejoices at someone's fall, ה׳ turns His anger away from the one who fell. So even the enemy's joy helps the sick person heal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: 'When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he stumbles, let your heart not be glad. Otherwise ה׳ will see, it will be bad in His eyes, and He will turn His anger away from him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to explain why רבא wanted his enemies to hear that he was sick.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse warns that if you celebrate your enemy's downfall, ה׳ will remove His anger from the enemy. רבא applies this to himself: if his haters rejoice, ה׳'s anger will turn away from him and he will get better.

keyTerms.meaning: and He will turn His anger away from him

steps.whatToRemember: Hide an illness on the first day, and then publicize it. Friends will pray, and even enemies' gloating causes ה׳ to turn His anger away.

phrases.english: And it is written: 'When your enemy falls, do not rejoice,'
'and when he stumbles, let your heart not be glad,'
'lest the Lord see it and it be evil in His eyes,'
'and He turn His anger away from him.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רבא's request that his enemies rejoice.
steps.raayaObject: That an enemy's rejoicing helps the sick person

steps.title: שמואל's response to a bad dream
steps.stepSummary: When שמואל saw a bad dream, he quoted a verse saying that dreams speak falsehood, and so he dismissed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When שמואל saw a bad dream, he would say: 'And dreams speak falsehood.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves back to the topic of dreams. It tells how שמואל calmed himself after a bad dream by quoting a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל used the verse in זכריה, which says dreams are empty, to treat a bad dream as meaningless. This sets up the next step, where he does the opposite with a good dream.

phrases.aramaic: שְׁמוּאֵל כִּי הֲוָה חָזֵי חֶלְמָא בִּישָׁא
phrases.english: Shmuel, when he would see a bad dream,
would say: 'And dreams speak falsehood.'

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּאֵל כִּי הֲוָה חָזֵי חֶלְמָא בִּישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: how to view the truth of dreams.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bad dream can be dismissed as meaningless.

steps.title: שמואל's response to a good dream
steps.stepSummary: When שמואל saw a good dream, he rejected the idea that dreams are false. He quoted the verse in which ה׳ says He speaks to a נביא in a dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he saw a good dream, he would say: Do dreams really speak falsehood? But it is written, 'In a dream I speak with him!'
steps.whatsHappening: This completes שמואל's practice. With a good dream, he quoted a different verse showing that dreams can be true messages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His words are phrased as a question ('וכי... והכתיב'), but this is not a challenge by the גמרא. It is שמואל's own way of affirming that a good dream is real. The two verses he used set up רבא's contradiction in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: in a dream I speak with him

steps.confusionAlert: Even though this line sounds like a קשיא, it is part of שמואל's personal practice. He picks whichever verse leads to a good outcome.

phrases.english: When he would see a good dream,
he would say: And do dreams speak falsehood?
But it is written: 'In a dream I speak with him!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The flip side of Step 28. Same person, opposite kind of dream, opposite verse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A good dream can be treated as a true message from ה׳.

steps.title: רבא points out that the two verses contradict
steps.stepSummary: רבא sets the two verses side by side. One says ה׳ speaks through dreams, and the other says dreams speak falsehood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised a contradiction: It is written, 'In a dream I speak with him,' and it is written, 'And dreams speak falsehood!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא takes the two verses שמואל used and asks how both can be true. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If dreams are a channel of נבואה, how can a פסוק call them false? The question is not about שמואל personally. It is about the verses themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: raises a contradiction (sets two sources against each other)

phrases.english: Rava raised a contradiction:
It is written: 'In a dream I speak with him,'
and it is written: 'And dreams speak falsehood!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the two verses from Steps 28–29 into a formal contradiction.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One verse says dreams carry ה׳'s word, while the other says dreams are false. Both cannot be true in the same way.

steps.title: Angel dreams are true; demon dreams are false
steps.stepSummary: The contradiction is resolved by recognizing two sources of dreams. A dream sent through a מלאך is true, and a dream sent through a שד is false.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here the verse speaks of a dream that comes through an angel, and here it speaks of a dream that comes through a demon.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רבא's contradiction by assigning each verse to a different kind of dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two verses are not discussing the same dream. 'In a dream I speak with him' refers to dreams sent by an angel. 'Dreams speak falsehood' refers to dreams caused by a demon. Both verses are correct.
steps.whatToRemember: Some dreams are true messages through a מלאך, and some are meaningless dreams from a שד.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
here, by means of an angel;
here, by means of a demon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 30.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (each verse refers to a different source of dream)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both verses describe all dreams, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each verse describes a different kind of dream: angel dreams are true, and demon dreams are false.

steps.title: Twenty-four interpreters, and every reading came true
steps.stepSummary: Through a long chain of transmitters, רבי בנאה reports that he took one dream to all 24 dream interpreters in ירושלים. Each gave a different interpretation, and every one came true for him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A long chain of sages quotes an elder, רבי בנאה, who said: There were 24 dream interpreters in ירושלים. Once I had a dream, and I went to all of them. Each one interpreted it differently from the others, and all of their interpretations came true for me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a personal story about dream interpretation, passed down through a long chain of teachers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key point is that one dream had 24 different meanings, and all of them happened. This shows that the interpretation itself shapes what the dream brings about. The next step states this as a principle.

keyTerms.meaning: in the name of a certain elder

phrases.english: Rabbi Bizna bar Zavda said
that Rabbi Akiva said
that Rabbi Panda said
that Rav Nachum said

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי בִּירִים מִשּׁוּם זָקֵן אֶחָד,
phrases.english: that Rabbi Birayim said in the name of one elder,
and who is he? Rabbi Bena'a:

phrases.aramaic: עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה פּוֹתְרֵי חֲלוֹמוֹת הָיוּ בִּירוּשָׁלַיִם,
phrases.english: There were twenty-four interpreters of dreams in Jerusalem.
Once I dreamed a dream
and I went to all of them.
And what this one interpreted for me
that one did not interpret for me,
and all of them were fulfilled in me.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי בִּיזְנָא בַּר זַבְדָּא אָמַר רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new idea about dreams: the power of interpretation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Different interpretations of one dream can all come true.

steps.title: All dreams follow the mouth
steps.stepSummary: רבי בנאה's experience fulfills the principle that all dreams follow the mouth of the interpreter.
steps.simpleTranslation: This fulfills what is said: 'All dreams follow the mouth.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story is tied to a principle that explains it: a dream turns out according to how it is interpreted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the interpreter's words shape the outcome, 24 different readings could all come true. This principle is why it matters who interprets a dream and how.
steps.confusionAlert: Although it is introduced with 'שנאמר,' the phrase 'כל החלומות הולכים אחר הפה' is not an actual פסוק. The גמרא itself will raise this question next and find its source elsewhere.
steps.whatToRemember: A dream's outcome follows its interpretation: כל החלומות הולכים אחר הפה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This principle stands behind many later teachings about dreams: be careful which interpreter you go to, and try to have a dream interpreted for the good.

phrases.english: to fulfill that which is said:
'All dreams follow the mouth.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the principle that explains רבי בנאה's story.
steps.raayaObject: That every interpretation of the dream came true
steps.raayaSupportSource: The saying 'כל החלומות הולכים אחר הפה'

steps.title: Is 'All Dreams Follow the Mouth' Really a Verse?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the wording of the previous step, which quoted 'all dreams follow the mouth' as if it were a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is 'all dreams follow the mouth' a verse?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the last step. It quoted 'all dreams follow the mouth' as something 'that is said' (שנאמר), but this exact phrase is not found in תנ"ך.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 33 introduced the rule with 'to fulfill what is said,' language normally used for a פסוק. The challenge is that no such פסוק exists word for word. The גמרא is setting up its answer that the rule is learned from a פסוק, even though it is not a direct quote.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (a challenging question)
Follow the mouth, meaning follow the interpreter's words

phrases.english: Is that to say that "all dreams follow the mouth"
phrases.notes: Quoting the phrase from the previous step

phrases.english: is a verse?
phrases.notes: The previous step treated it like a quoted verse

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ ״כׇּל הַחֲלוֹמוֹת הוֹלְכִים אַחַר הַפֶּה״ קְרָא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wording used in the proof of step 33
steps.kashyaTarget: The phrase 'all dreams follow the mouth' being quoted as 'what is said' (a verse)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The phrase does not appear in תנ"ך, so it cannot be called a fulfillment of 'what is said'

steps.title: Yes, It Comes From a Verse About יוסף
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the rule is indeed rooted in a פסוק, as רבי אלעזר derived it from the שר המשקים's words about יוסף.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, and this follows רבי אלעזר. רבי אלעזר said: From where do we know that all dreams follow the mouth? As it says: 'And it happened, just as he interpreted for us, so it was.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers yes. The rule is based on a פסוק, as רבי אלעזר showed from the story of יוסף interpreting the dreams of פרעה's two officers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שר המשקים told פרעה that whatever יוסף interpreted is exactly what happened. רבי אלעזר reads this as: the interpretation itself caused the result. So the rule is not a direct quote, but it is a teaching drawn from a פסוק, which is enough to call it 'what is said.'

phrases.english: Yes, and it is in line with Rabbi Elazar.
phrases.notes: Confirms there is a verse behind the rule

phrases.english: For Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: מִנַּיִן שֶׁכָּל הַחֲלוֹמוֹת הוֹלְכִין אַחַר הַפֶּה?
phrases.english: From where do we know that all dreams follow the mouth?

phrases.aramaic: — שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וַיְהִי כַּאֲשֶׁר פָּתַר לָנוּ כֵּן הָיָה״.
phrases.english: As it is said: "And it came to pass, as he interpreted for us, so it was."
phrases.notes: בראשית 41:13, the שר המשקים speaking to פרעה about יוסף

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 34
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies the verse that serves as the source of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rule is a phrase with no verse behind it
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule is derived from 'as he interpreted for us, so it was'

steps.title: רבא's Limit: The Interpretation Must Fit the Dream
steps.stepSummary: רבא limits the rule: a dream follows the interpretation only when the interpretation matches the content of the dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: This is only when he interprets it in a way that fits his dream, as it says: 'Each man according to his dream he interpreted.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a condition to the rule. An interpretation only takes effect if it actually fits what was seen in the dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without this limit, someone could think any random interpretation, even one unrelated to the dream, would come true. רבא proves from the פסוק that יוסף interpreted each officer's dream according to its own content. So the interpreter's power works only within what the dream reasonably means.

keyTerms.meaning: Similar to his dream, fitting its content

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a key boundary for the whole idea that dreams follow the interpretation: the meaning must come from the dream itself.

phrases.english: Rava said:
And this is only when it is interpreted for him in a way that fits his dream,
as it is said: "Each man according to his dream he interpreted."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: וְהוּא דִּמְפַשַּׁר לֵיהּ מֵעֵין חֶלְמֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limiting condition to רבי אלעזר's rule
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A dream follows the interpretation only when the interpretation fits the dream's content

steps.title: How Did the Baker Know the Interpretation Was Good?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the שר האופים knew that יוסף's interpretation of the butler's dream was correct.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And the chief baker saw' that the interpretation was good. How did he know?
steps.whatsHappening: Still on the story of יוסף, the גמרא asks a question on the פסוק. How could the שר האופים tell that יוסף's interpretation was a good one?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the baker 'saw' that the interpretation was good, as if he had a way to check it. But he was just hearing יוסף explain someone else's dream. The גמרא wants to know what gave him this certainty.

phrases.english: "And the chief baker saw" (that the interpretation was good),
From where did he know?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a related question on the same story of יוסף and the officers
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the baker knew יוסף's interpretation was correct

steps.title: Each Officer Also Saw the Other's Interpretation
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר answers that each officer was shown in his own dream the interpretation of the other officer's dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: This teaches that each one was shown his own dream and the interpretation of his friend's dream.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question. In the dream, each officer saw his own dream plus the meaning of the other one's dream.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So when יוסף explained the butler's dream, the baker already knew the true meaning from his own dream. Since יוסף's words matched what he had seen, the baker knew יוסף was right. This also connects to the next idea, a dream interpreted inside a dream.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:
This teaches that each and every one
phrases.notes: Both the butler and the baker

phrases.english: was shown his own dream
and the interpretation of his fellow's dream.
phrases.notes: That is how the baker could check יוסף's interpretation

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 37
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each officer saw the interpretation of the other's dream, so the baker could recognize יוסף's correct interpretation

steps.title: A Verse on Waking Is a Small Prophecy
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that if a person wakes up and a פסוק suddenly comes to his mouth, it is a minor נבואה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: If someone woke up early and a פסוק fell into his mouth, this is a small prophecy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching of רבי יוחנן about signs from Heaven. A פסוק that pops into one's mouth on waking is a minor form of נבואה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is similar to a dream: a message that comes to a person without planning. The content of that פסוק hints at what will happen to him. It continues the theme that some messages at night or on waking carry real meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: A verse fell into his mouth, came to him on its own

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: הִשְׁכִּים וְנָפַל לוֹ פָּסוּק לְתוֹךְ פִּיו,
phrases.english: If one woke up and a verse fell into his mouth,
phrases.notes: Without trying to think of it

phrases.english: this is a minor prophecy.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הִשְׁכִּים וְנָפַל לוֹ פָּסוּק לְתוֹךְ פִּיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New teaching on the related theme of meaningful messages
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A פסוק that comes to one's mouth on waking is a minor נבואה

steps.title: Three Kinds of Dreams That Come True
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן lists three dreams that are fulfilled: a morning dream, a dream a friend had about you, and a dream interpreted within the dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Three dreams come true: a dream of the morning, a dream that his friend dreamed about him, and a dream that was interpreted inside a dream.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a list of three types of dreams that are especially likely to come true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא simply lists these three types without explaining why each one comes true. The third type, a dream interpreted inside the dream, recalls פרעה's officers in the previous steps, who were each shown an interpretation within their dreams.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said,
three dreams are fulfilled:
a dream of the morning,
and a dream that his fellow dreamed about him,
and a dream that was interpreted within a dream.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, שְׁלֹשָׁה חֲלוֹמוֹת מִתְקַיְּימִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching of רבי יוחנן on meaningful dreams
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A morning dream, a dream about you by a friend, and a dream interpreted within a dream come true

steps.title: Some Add: A Repeated Dream Also Comes True
steps.stepSummary: A יש אומר adds a fourth type: a dream that repeats itself, proven from פרעה's doubled dream.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some say: also a dream that is repeated, as it says: 'And because the dream was repeated...'
steps.whatsHappening: Another opinion adds to רבי יוחנן's list. A dream that comes again also comes true.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is from יוסף's words to פרעה: the dream came twice because the matter is firmly set by ה׳. Repetition shows the message is fixed and will happen.
steps.whatToRemember: Dreams follow the interpretation only if it fits the dream (רבא). Dreams that come true: morning dreams, a dream a friend had about you, a dream interpreted within a dream, and according to some, a repeated dream.

phrases.english: And some say:
also a dream that is repeated,
as it is said: "And because the dream was repeated, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fourth item to רבי יוחנן's list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A repeated dream also comes true, based on פרעה's doubled dream

steps.title: Dreams show only what a person was thinking about
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני, quoting רבי יונתן, teaches that a person is shown in his dreams only the thoughts of his own heart. He proves it from דניאל's words to נבוכדנצר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמואל בר נחמני said that רבי יונתן said: A person is shown in a dream only what came from the thoughts of his heart. As the verse says: 'You, O king, your thoughts came up on your bed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about dreams. A dream reflects what a person was thinking about while awake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps were about which dreams come true. This step adds something about where dreams come from: a person's own thoughts. The proof is that דניאל told נבוכדנצר his dream came from the thoughts he had while lying in bed.

keyTerms.meaning: They show (a person, in a dream)
As it is said (introduces a פסוק as proof)

steps.whyThisMatters: This explains why many dreams are not meaningful messages. Often they simply replay what a person was thinking about.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani said
that Rabbi Yonatan said:
A person is not shown (in a dream)
anything except the thoughts of his heart.
As it is said: 'You, O king,'
phrases.notes: דניאל 2:29, where דניאל speaks to נבוכדנצר

phrases.english: 'your thoughts came up upon your bed.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from which dreams are fulfilled (steps 40-41) to where dreams come from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person's dreams are built only from his own waking thoughts.

steps.title: A second verse proving the same idea
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא offers another verse from the same passage in דניאל to prove that dreams come from a person's thoughts.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say the proof comes from here instead: 'And you will know the thoughts of your heart.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, alternative source for the teaching of רבי יונתן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The next verse says the dream was shown so the king would 'know the thoughts of his heart.' That means the dream revealed what was already inside his mind. This supports the same rule as the first verse, using a different פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces an alternative answer or source)

steps.confusionAlert: 'ואיבעית אימא' does not mean the first proof was wrong. It just offers another way to prove the same point.

phrases.english: And if you wish, say (the proof is) from here:
'And the thoughts of your heart you will know.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an alternative verse to prove the teaching in step 42.
steps.raayaObject: That dreams reflect a person's own thoughts

steps.title: Proof from experience: no one dreams of impossible things
steps.stepSummary: רבא supports the idea from common experience. People never dream of a golden palm tree or an elephant going through the eye of a needle, because they never think about such things.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Know that this is true, because a person is never shown in a dream a golden palm tree, or an elephant going through the eye of a needle.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא adds a proof from everyday life that dreams come only from a person's own thoughts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If dreams came from outside a person's mind, people would sometimes dream of strange, impossible things. Since nobody dreams of a golden palm tree or an elephant passing through a needle's eye, dreams must be built from what a person already imagines. This is a logical proof, not a verse.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that this is so); introduces a supporting proof

steps.whatToRemember: Dreams come from a person's own thoughts. This is proven from two verses in דניאל and from רבא's observation that no one dreams of things he has never imagined.
steps.whyThisMatters: 'An elephant through the eye of a needle' became a well-known Talmudic image for something unthinkable.

phrases.english: Rava said: Know (that this is so),
for a person is not shown (in a dream)
neither a palm tree of gold
nor an elephant going
through the eye of a needle.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a proof from experience to the verse-based proofs in steps 42-43.
steps.raayaObject: That dreams come only from a person's own thoughts
steps.raayaSupportSource: Common experience: no one dreams of impossible things he has never imagined
